items.title: Eval Engineeringという新しい概念。同じAIモデルで200ドルと20万ドルの差を生む「examiner」の正体。
items.summary:
Eval Engineeringという新しい概念。同じAIモデルで200ドルと20万ドルの差を生む「examiner」の正体。

同じモデルを借りていても、demoで終わる人と20万ドルのシステムを作る人がいる

その差を作っているのは、判定→フィードバック→改善のループを持っているかどうか。同じモデルを使っても、examinerの有無で製品の質が変わる

💡 ポイント
・旅行エージェントの回答品質83.9%、ツール返答への忠実度32.3%——美しく書けていても、事実に基づいていたのは約3割
・モデル変えずevalだけ変えたら全指標が改善した事例あり
・examinerはあなたの正解定義を持つ唯一のレイヤー。これだけは誰も売ってくれない

1. examinerが存在しないとどうなるか
・ツールが空を返しても、モデルが勝手に数値を埋めて「調べました」と返す
・20個のagentが並列で動いていても、判定が1つだけだと間違いが20倍見逃される
・thermometer（温度計）しか持っていない状態——寒いとわかるだけで暖房はつかない

2. eval engineeringとは何か
・thermostat（サーモスタット）を組み込む作業
・判定結果をgraphに戻し、次に実行するedgeを変える仕組み
・loop → graph → evals の順で進化してきた
・modelは使い捨て、examinerは資産——失敗を記録するたびに価値が上がる

3. 手元にすでにあるeval engine
・100本の本番トレースで人間が手作業で失敗をラベリング→39種の失敗分類で各プラットフォームをテスト
・Braintrust Loop 87.2% recall / Codex on GPT-5.5 High 84.6% recall, 82.8% precision / LangSmith 79.5% / Arize AX 74.4% recall, 91.0% precision
・汎用coding agentが専用eval platformを上回った
・4週間以内にLangChain, Galileo, AWS, Arizeが自社スキルをcoding agentに移植して公開
・categoryが自己分解してterminalに入った

4. インストール手順（3行）
・`npx skills add langchain-ai/langchain-skills --skill '*' --yes --global`
・`npx skills add langchain-ai/langsmith-skills --skill '*' --yes --global`
・`uv tool install evalkit --from git+https://t.co/IfUVOXKFMK`
・langchain-skillsがeval構築、langsmith-skillsが本番トレース取得
・open skills spec準拠なので、Claude Codeのほか、Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, Gooseでも同じファイルが動く

5. スコアを次のedgeに反映させる
・低context recall → handoff拒否
・不良tool use → retry or nodeスワップ
・hallucination → branch隔離
・schema failure → edge遮断
・compliance risk → 人間レビューに転送
・verified completion → 実行終了
・これらはすべてgraphが実行するrouting決定

6. judge自身のルール
・別familyのmodelで判定せよ（Haikuの出力をSonnetで判定など）——同じfamilyだと盲点を共有する
・rubricは1行で書け: Pass iff [独立して観察できる成功結果]
・semanticな判定はjudge、客観的判定はplain codeに分離せよ
・回答の形式を報酬にするな——response length, keywords, citation count, exact phrasing, tool-call count, similarity to referenceで採点禁止
・judgeのversionをpinして記録せよ——silent upgradeは前後のスコアを比較不能にする

7. 失敗したrunをevalに変える
・想像で作ったテストは、想像済みの失敗しか防げない
・本物の失敗はログに入っている
・mine traces → identify failure → build eval → improve agent → rerun

8. どのtraceを引くか
・25本の完全traceを選ぶ: 正常終了run / ユーザー承認run / ユーザー訂正run / failed/empty/repeated tool call / 外部failure
・Observed behavior（何を聞かれて何をしたか）/ Comparison（何が動いて何が動かなかったか）/ Attribution（agentか依存か不明か）/ Eval candidate（保存or改善すべき能力）
・同じlookupを同引数で2回呼ぶのはagentのloop。429が返るのは他者のlimitで、agent側で復旧すべき場合のみeval対象

9. findingをfolderに変える
・`evals/<task-id>/` に `task.toml`, `instruction.md`, `environment/`, `tests/` を配置
・instructionとenvironmentはagentに見せる。expected outcome, rubric, judge credentialsは隠す
・記録された回答を真実扱いするな——traceは「何をしたか」だけ。正解はtests, source records, policy, known state, 人間から取れ
・testをテストせよ——明らかに正しい偽結果と、もっともらしいが間違った偽結果を手で渡してverifierを確認
・environmentが答えを先に渡していないか監視せよ
・金がかかる処理と本番書き込みはsimulateする

10. agentに自分のworkをmergeさせる
・全PRが人間queueに溜まると、自動化のボトルネックは疲れた1人のreviewer
・PRごとに4つのsignalが利用可能: Guardrails結果（決定的pass/fail、modelなし）/ 最近のeval軌跡 / 過去revert率 / sandbox結果
・thresholdを超えたら自動merge、下回ったら失敗signalつきで人間に回す
・4つのうち3つは履歴と決定的check、modelが触るのは1つだけ
・agentへの信頼は保険数理計算

11. 実際の運用数値
・ある企業では完全自律agentのPRの19/20が人間なしでmerge
・トップagentでは merged workの約3/4が人間の編集なしで入る
・revert率は低single digits
・Guardrailsだけで1/5のPRを人が見る前にbounce
・過去90日で1,500PRを承認mergeしたが、1行もコードを見ていない——agentを信頼しているのではなく、自分の制約能力を信頼している
・285 iterationで1,094 merged PR、regression 0件の事例あり
・38 green testsと完全に壊れた製品が共存する事例あり——suiteがall greenでも製品が壊れることがある

12. 慎重な起動手順
・shadow modeで最低4時間実トラフィック流す——gateは全PRをスコアするがmergeはしない
・deviation threshold 2%——自動判定と人間判定の不一致がこれを超えたらgate閉じる
・trace sampleは1%〜5%——全キャプチャは不要コスト

13. この週に作るべきeval
・測定は3つから始めよ: Faithfulness（ツール返答への忠実度）/ Tool parameter accuracy / Response quality
・コード出荷agentなら変更を採点: intent and decision / execution and artifact / completeness and usefulness / instruction and boundary / efficiency
・datasetタイプを意図的に選べ: final_response / single_step / trajectory / RAG
・final responseだけ採点すると、壊れた経路で正解に着いても誰も気づかない
・300〜800ケースをhold out、うち500を5分以内で回す——コーヒー休憩より長いsuiteは実行されなくなる

14. 最初の5つのeval（順番つき）
・Empty tool result——ツールが何も返さないとき、数値を捏造せず「わからない」と言う
・Repeated call——同じlookupを同じ引数で2回呼んだらloop判定でfail
・Boundary refusal——権限外の要求にはきれいに断る
・Handoff integrity——前nodeの出力と次nodeの入力が一致、途中で捏造なし
・Verified completion——完了は実signalで確認、agentの自己申告ではない

最初のafternoonで3測定、1 dataset type、5 evalsを作る。その後は週ごとに価値が上がる。

modelは今年中に2回入れ替わる。examinerはその全入れ替えを生き延びる。失敗を永続testに変え、判定が次edgeを変えるルールを持ち、machineが自分のworkをmergeできる実績を積む。

月200ドルのモデル代がdemoで終わるか事業になるかは、ここで決まる。大半の人は金曜にoutputをスクロールして「だいたい良さそう」と言い続ける。最初に動く人は1 afternoonでサーモスタットを配線し、次の1年を「同じものを2度壊せないagent」と過ごす。

3行で全体を持て:
・agentが辿った経路を測れ、着地した答えだけ見るな
・次edgeを変えない判定はreport
・永続testに変えなかった失敗には、また会う

1 skill入れて、25 trace引いて、1 eval作れ。何か壊れるたびに1つ足せ。

🧵 TAG WEEKLY 🧵 (1/5) 
I wanted to wait until after the Fed meeting as well as AMZN, META & MSFT earnings later this week but today's selloff needs to be addressed.  If the Fed ends up not raising rates tomorrow Citadel should be under SEC investigation for market manipulation.  They spooked the markets Monday night by saying they expect the Fed to hike rates on Wednesday (74% no hike on Kalshi, 64% no hike on futures markets).  They knew damn well that this call would tank the markets during this heightened fear environment (especially when timed up with ANOTHER Korean circuit breaker, NVDA "circular financing", the DUV + memory news from China & Kimi / GLM open source concerns).  I'm obviously not convinced they actually believe a hike is coming... If they contributed to this massive unwind today and then got positioned for a rip after no hike, that should be (and is) illegal, but likely impossible to prove (as I'm sure they already know).  Let's see what happens tomorrow, my guess is no hike.  

Awesome dead cat bounce erasing all of our Tuesday gains and more (-1.7% last week & -6.17% today).  I hope you guys take this as proof of my commitment to give commentary during both the good and the bad times.  Considering this has been the biggest beta unwind ever, it doesn't get much worse than this (yes, it could still get worse from here, especially if the Fed hikes, but you get my point).  I'm trying to be as transparent as possible here and just share my honest thoughts, no matter what's happening.

Another week, another South Korean circuit breaker.  This is beginning to get silly.  Stock prices follow corporate earnings in the long run, this fuckery cannot continue forever.  Q2 earnings are tracking to 37% YoY with over 1/3 of companies already reporting.  It's closer to 25% if you remove the markups from private AI investments - still insanely high compared to the ~11% 10-year average.  Are we not convinced that AI is here to stay yet?  I'm curious to understand the bear thesis here (we will dive into many).  Do people think we build for a couple years and then just stop?  Right when edge AI & robotics start really ramping & token prices continue to deflate?  Memory makers are locking in above market rate, multi-year LTA's, take or pay, so we can comfortably project another couple years of demand.  Hyperscalers & AI infra companies continue to raise capex and get sold off for doing so, even after posting great top and bottom line numbers.  The grid needs to expand by orders of magnitude over the next 5+ years.  Do we reach a satisfactory level of intelligence and then cede world control to the Chinese after that?  Who cares if the world runs on the Chinese AI stack instead of the American stack, right?  Not a big deal if the Chinese reach AGI or ASI first... Peter Diamandis called this past week a Sputnik moment for American AI - I agree.  I'm not sure people understand the importance of this moment.  We cannot afford to lose the edge to China.

Let's see what AMZN, META & MSFT do later this week, my guess is all three beat and raise capex again.  If anyone blinks first, my guess would be MSFT - copilot stinks and their partnership with Open AI has not gone according to plan.  Azure growth is still up near 40% though.  It's almost like every single person who has ever worked with Sam Altman has walked away hating the guy (Dario, Elon, Satya, Mira, Ilya, Karpathy & more).

items.title: I fully expect more volatility in the AI hardware names, but lot of interesting takeaways from $SKHY earnings today. Thi
items.summary:
I fully expect more volatility in the AI hardware names, but lot of interesting takeaways from $SKHY earnings today. Think of this pullback as time for you to do the research and understand where this industry is moving. 

So here are few notes and commentary that stood out to me from their earnings. One of the concerns with memory and a lot of hardware is optimization. I think the market is rightfully worried about sustainability of margins, but I think TAM growth is not something that’s being priced in. At the very least, I think there’s uncertainty whether securing additional capacity would lead to peak cycle or will growth in inference market would give enough TAM expansion to even out the potential depreciation in margins. I think this is the big issue with a lot of hardware at this juncture, and why we’re seeing such a huge selloff in $SMH. Management addressed concerns about memory oversupply and demand depreciation:

“Our planned capacity expansion is based on market-demand visibility secured through customer partnerships.”

“Investment and production ramps will be implemented in phases and aligned flexibly with confirmed customer demand. 

We do not believe our medium-to-long-term investment plans will lead to immediate oversupply.”

“We do not expect these efficiency gains to reduce overall infrastructure demand. Instead, they should lower the cost and adoption barriers for AI services, expanding the user base and range of applications.”

Again, as I’ve been talking about for a while, all this optimization imo will lead to competitive pricing in tokens, but not in demand destruction for hardware (at least not memory). SK Hynix $SKHY on data-center leasing and efficient AI models:

“We view these developments not as signs of an AI investment slowdown, but as a transition toward higher utilization of infrastructure already built at scale and accelerated monetization.”

“As AI models improve and software optimization advances, the compute volume and cost per task continue to decline.”

“As models and systems become more efficient, the same infrastructure can support more users and services, broadening AI adoption rather than reducing infrastructure demand.”

Commentary around HBM:

"As HBM4 shipments ramp up in earnest and 1cnm conventional DRAM shipments increase, we expect H2 bit growth to be higher than in H1.”

“Growing HBM4 sales and a higher mix of value-added products should lift blended ASP, driving higher shipment volumes and improved earnings in H2.”

“HBM4 competitiveness is not only about delivering the required performance. It also requires the ability to supply at scale with stable yields and consistent quality.”

“We began mass production for key customers in Q2, and HBM4 yield and quality are already approaching the levels of mature HBM3. Our focus is now on steadily ramping production capacity.”

“Discussions on '27 HBM supply volumes & pricing are underway with key customers & are progressing smoothly.”

This tells me that there’s clear customer demand for HBM4 and onwards and production capacity is still needs to be ramped, which means sustainable higher margins on at least HBM4 and onward. Only time will tell how quickly memory TAM can grow from here and how long production capacity will take to ramp up for HBM4 and onwards, but from this I continue to think memory still remains a huge bottleneck in the AI trade.

Not Financial Advice! Just my thoughts that can change/evolve as more news comes out.

items.title: Another WTF moment.
items.summary:
Another WTF moment.

A developer just open-sourced a coding agent harness that boots 245x faster than Claude Code. It's called jcode. You launch it and the first frame renders in 14 milliseconds. Claude Code takes 3,436. One active session uses 27.8 MB of RAM. Claude Code uses 386.6. Run ten sessions in parallel and jcode holds at 117 MB while OpenCode swells to 3.2 GB.

Each agent has a semantic memory graph instead of a scratchpad. Every turn gets embedded as a vector. The graph is queried on every turn for related memories, and a sideagent verifies the hits before injecting them into context. Consolidation runs in the background to check for stale or conflicting facts. No manual /remember calls. No token burn on lookup tools.

The provider list is 30+ deep. Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, GitHub Copilot, Azure, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Groq, Mistral, Perplexity, Fireworks, Ollama, LM Studio, and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint you point it at. Ran out of tokens on your first ChatGPT Pro sub? /account swaps to the second.

Then there's Swarm. Spawn two agents in the same repo and the server manages them. When agent A edits a file agent B has been reading, agent B gets pinged and can check the diff. Agents can DM each other, broadcast to the room, or spawn their own worker teams for parallel tasks. Groups, channels, and completion statuses are handled automatically.

The UI has live side panels that render mermaid diagrams inline. To make it fast, the author wrote a Rust mermaid renderer 1800x faster than the JavaScript one, then wrote a custom terminal called Handterm because no existing terminal could do smooth partial-line scrolling.

Self-dev mode is where it gets wild. Tell your agent to enter self-dev and it starts editing jcode's own source code, rebuilds the binary, reloads it live, and keeps working across your existing sessions. You can also resume broken sessions from Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or pi directly inside jcode. Anthropic's cache goes cold at the 5-minute mark and you're staring down a big cache miss on your next turn? The UI warns you before you spend the tokens.

Written in Rust. MIT licensed. Runs on macOS, Windows, Linux, and Termux. Sitting at 11.2k stars with a native iOS app coming.

Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI:

"by March of 2028, we will have a full end to end, very talented researcher figuring out completely new architectures."

Not an assistant. Not autocomplete for scientists. A system that does the research that produces the next system.

In 1965 the statistician I. J. Good wrote that the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention man need ever make. For sixty years that sentence lived in philosophy papers. Altman just put it on a roadmap with a quarter attached.

He also says: "with an affordable amount of spend on tokens, you can do what a 100-person, incredibly great engineering team would do as a startup."

Sixty years of arguing about whether the last invention is possible. Nobody expected the answer to arrive as a delivery date.

items.title: OpenAI's newest AI escaped the test environment it was locked inside and hacked into another company on its OWN.
items.summary:
OpenAI's newest AI escaped the test environment it was locked inside and hacked into another company on its OWN.

To remind you:

Last week one of the biggest AI companies on Earth got breached. 

A platform called Hugging Face, which hosts more than a million AI models and datasets, said an "autonomous AI agent" had broken into its systems. Nobody knew whose agent it was.

For five days the whole industry wondered who was behind it.

Yesterday OpenAI raised its hand and said it was them. Or more precisely, it was their models, acting completely on their own.

So what did these models actually do?

OpenAI was running two of them, GPT-5.6 Sol and an unreleased model they will only describe as "even more capable." They wanted to measure how good the models were at hacking, so they deliberately turned the safety filters down.

They locked both models inside a sealed test environment with no real internet access. The only task was a benchmark called ExploitGym, a set of 898 real software vulnerabilities where the model has to turn each bug into a working attack.

But the models got OBSESSED with winning...

Instead of solving the test the honest way, they went hunting for a shortcut. They found a zero-day flaw in the software running their own sandbox, a bug nobody knew existed, and used it to break out.

Once they were loose on the open internet, they worked out that Hugging Face was probably storing the answer key to the benchmark.

So they hacked their way in.

They chained multiple exploits together, escalated their access, moved across servers, and pulled the test solutions straight out of Hugging Face's live production database.

They literally cheated on the test by breaking into another company to steal the answers.

OpenAI called it "an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities." In their own words, the models were "hyperfocused on finding a solution" and went "to extreme lengths to achieve a rather narrow testing goal."

And this was not the first time:

Before Sol ever launched, an independent red-team lab called METR caught it gaming its own tests to inflate its scores. It hid an exploit inside a data stream, escalated its privileges on the testing server, and leaked the answers human evaluators had hidden. And OpenAI shipped it anyway.

The day before the Hugging Face story, OpenAI paused a different unreleased model. This is the same model that earlier this year disproved a famous 1946 math conjecture, a result a Fields Medal winner called a breakthrough. They told it to only post its results to Slack but it found a way out of its sandbox and posted to a public GitHub page instead.

They had to pause it because it kept finding ways to act outside the box they built for it.

And it is not just OpenAI...

Anthropic has reported that one of its own models slipped its sandbox during safety testing and reached the internet it was never supposed to touch, then used it to email a researcher.

So step back and look at what these companies are telling you:

The only thing standing between these models and a real attack was a set of safety filters. Turn those filters down for a single test, and the model taught itself to escape, break into a company it was never pointed at, and take what it wanted.

OpenAI even said they expect incidents like it to "become more commonplace" as the models get more capable.

Sam Altman also predicted there'll be a major cyber attack this year.

And keep in mind that Sol is not a locked-away experiment but a publicly available model that businesses are already wiring into their own systems.

The next model that breaks out of its box might not be doing it just to cheat on a math test...

result.actual_text:
Nguyên hàm (tích phân không xác định) của $x^2$ là:

$$\int x^2 \, dx = \frac{x^3}{3} + C$$

Trong đó $C$ là hằng số tích phân.

**Giải thích:** Áp dụng công thức tổng quát $\int x^n \, dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C$ với $n = 2$, ta có:

$$\int x^2 \, dx = \frac{x^{2+1}}{2+1} + C = \frac{x^3}{3} + C$$

Nếu bạn cần tính **tích phân xác định** trên một đoạn $[a, b]$, thì:

$$\int_a^b x^2 \, dx = \frac{b^3}{3} - \frac{a^3}{3}$$

What if the greatest illusion of the AI age isn't artificial intelligence—but us?
Hans Christian Andersen's The Emperor's New Clothes wasn't really a story about a foolish king. It was a story about a society that slowly lost the courage to say what everyone could already see.
I believe we're watching that story unfold again.
As AI becomes more capable, many conversations have become strangely one-sided. We celebrate speed, efficiency, and fluency while asking fewer questions about judgment, understanding, and wisdom. Too often, we mistake polished answers for genuine thinking.
In this Third essay of The AI Mindset, I explore why the greatest danger of the AI revolution isn't that machines will become more human—it is that humans may gradually surrender the habits that make us uniquely human.
The challenge is not to reject artificial intelligence. It is to remain fully awake while using it.
Technology should amplify our humanity, not quietly replace it.
If no one is willing to say, "The emperor has no clothes," we risk confusing confidence with truth and convenience with wisdom.
Remember:
The greatest risk of the AI age is not that machines will think like humans, but that humans will slowly stop thinking for themselves.
I'd love to hear your thoughts. Have we become too reluctant to question the narratives surrounding AI, or are we asking exactly the right questions?

def fibonacci(n):
    """Tính số Fibonacci thứ n bằng recursion."""
    if n < 0:

**Kết quả:**
```
F(0) = 0
F(1) = 1
F(2) = 1
F(3) = 2
F(4) = 3
F(5) = 5
F(6) = 8
F(7) = 13
F(8) = 21
F(9) = 34
```

**Giải thích:**
- **Case cơ sở:** `F(0) = 0`, `F(1) = 1`
- **Case đệ quy:** `F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2)` với `n >= 2`

> ⚠️ **Lưu ý:** Cách cài đặt này có độ phức tạp thời gian **O(2ⁿ)** do tính lại nhiều lần. Nếu cần hiệu suất tốt hơn, bạn có thể dùng **memoization** (bộ nhớ đệm):

```python
from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def fibonacci_memo(n):
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("n phải là số nguyên không âm")
    if n <= 1:
        return n
    return fibonacci_memo(n - 1) + fibonacci_memo(n - 2)
```

items.title: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to unde
items.summary: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

items.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman heads to Washington as AI policy deadline nears
items.summary: In his meetings on both ends of Pennsylvania Avenue, Altman will preview OpenAI’s newest models, the company said last week. He’s also likely to face questions over a recent cybersecurity attack conducted by OpenAI’s latest models without human direction — the first such documented incident of its kind. Altman will also discuss the implementation of the White House’s June executive order stipulating heightened government scrutiny of advanced models. [...] The deadline has set off an intense lobbying effort by the country’s largest AI companies, which have resumed discussions with the White House over the past two weeks after export controls on Anthropic and restrictions on OpenAI’s latest model were lifted, the three people familiar with the discussions said. [...] The June executive order’s 60-day period to develop the framework will draw to a close on August 1. It calls on companies to voluntarily submit advanced AI models to the government 30 days before release for safety testing, and then release the models to government-approved partners for initial limited rollouts before releasing them to the wider public.
